extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, evolutionary biologists, and scientifically literate general readers assessing evidence for species-change
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether the geological and palaeontological record supports gradual change by natural selection — including what kinds of intermediate forms to expect, how to interpret absence of fossils, and how geological processes affect preservation. Intended to help judge the evidential weight of fossil occurrences, stratigraphic gaps, and rates of geological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect intermediates relative to common progenitor, not necessarily between derived forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “we should always look for forms intermediate between each species and a common but unknown progenitor; and the progenitor will generally have differed in some respects from all its modified descendants.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect direct intermediate forms combining the distinctive characters of two highly modified descendant species. Instead, look for forms intermediate between each species and their shared (often unknown) ancestor. Example: fantail and pouter pigeons are each intermediate to the rock-pigeon, but there need not be a form directly combining both derived traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of intermediate links is explained by extreme imperfection of the geological record
rubrics_metrics.description: “The geological record, viewed as a whole, is extremely imperfect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat gaps in stratigraphic sequences as expected rather than fatal to a theory of gradual change. Consider preservation bias, limited exploration, intermittence of deposition, dissolution after uplift, and long blank intervals between formations before concluding intermediates never existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect an enormous number of former intermediate/transitional links
rubrics_metrics.description: “the number of intermediate and transitional links, between all living and extinct species, must have been inconceivably great.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct theory should accommodate the expectation that countless transitional forms once existed but were mostly not preserved or have been destroyed — so absence in collections is plausible and compatible with gradual evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require vast lapse of geological time to make slow change plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that the slow process of modification by natural selection requires incomprehensibly vast past periods of time (Lyell referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging plausibility of slow evolution, use geological indicators (thickness of sedimentary piles, denudation evidence, rates of deposition/erosion) to estimate whether sufficient time has elapsed. Empirical rates (e.g., Mississippi estimate, cliff erosion) and measured strata thicknesses provide lower-bound checks on required durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation bias: soft-bodied and many littoral/terrestrial organisms seldom fossilize
rubrics_metrics.description: “No organism wholly soft can be preserved. Shells and bones will decay and disappear when left on the bottom of the sea, where sediment is not accumulating.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for taxonomic and ecological biases in fossil preservation (soft parts, littoral species, terrestrial forms). The absence of certain groups (e.g., many littoral cirripedes, land-shells, mammals in older strata) may reflect preservational limits rather than actual absence in past faunas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poorness and sampling bias of palaeontological collections
rubrics_metrics.description: “Numbers of our fossil species are known and named from single and often broken specimens, or from a few specimens collected on some one spot. Only a small portion of the surface of the earth has been geologically explored.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat single or sparse occurrences cautiously. Recognize that collections are incomplete, geographically biased, and often based on accidental finds; avoid over-interpreting absence or rarity in museum records as reflecting historical scarcity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermittence of geological formations (wide gaps between successive formations)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the several formations being separated from each other by wide intervals of time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume stratigraphic continuity within a region. Gaps between formations mean that many intermediate faunas may have existed elsewhere or in intervals not preserved locally. Correlate widely across regions before inferring phyletic sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thick fossiliferous deposits are typically produced during subsidence and are required to resist later degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: “thick and extensive accumulations of sediment may be formed ... in profound depths of the sea ... or sediment may be accumulated ... over a shallow bottom, if it continue slowly to subside. I am convinced that all our ancient formations, which are rich in fossils, have thus been formed during subsidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depositional context: fossil-rich, thick strata usually reflect prolonged subsidence that maintained shallow, life-friendly conditions. Conversely, deposits formed on stationary or uplifted beds are more likely to be lost or barren; use depositional mechanism to judge completeness of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migration and geographic variability confound first/last appearances in a single locality
rubrics_metrics.description: “when we see a species first appearing in any formation, the probability is that it only then first immigrated into that area.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate first appearance in a particular section with time of origin, nor last appearance with extinction. Consider immigration/emigration and differing regional timings; cross-regional correlation is necessary to infer true origination or extinction events.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single formation need not display continuous gradation because deposition may be intermittent
rubrics_metrics.description: “a formation composed of beds of different mineralogical composition, we may reasonably suspect that the process of deposition has been much interrupted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect abrupt but possibly slight changes within formations rather than a perfect gradational series. Look for evidence of interruptions (changes in lithology, root-bearing horizons, multiple forest levels) that indicate non-continuous deposition and thus gaps in biological record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic practice affects perceived gaps between species and varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: “naturalists have no golden rule by which to distinguish species and varieties; they grant some little variability to each species, but when they meet with a somewhat greater amount of difference... they rank both as species, unless they are enabled to connect them together by close intermediate gradations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating apparent discontinuities, account for subjective taxonomic thresholds. Differences in how authors split versus lump taxa influence whether intermediates are recognized; be cautious about using taxonomic ranks as hard evidence of abrupt origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and replacement cause extermination of intermediate forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “the process of natural selection ... new varieties continually take the places of and exterminate their parent-forms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect many transitional forms to be short-lived and to be competitively excluded by their descendants or competitors; this ecological dynamic reduces the chance that intermediates are preserved and later discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-sea deposition preserves less evidence of life than shallow subsiding basins
rubrics_metrics.description: “in profound depths of the sea ... we may conclude that the bottom will be inhabited by extremely few animals, and the mass when upraised will give a most imperfect record of the forms of life which then existed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different depositional environments record biotas differently: deep-water deposits may produce thick sediment but poor fossil representation of life, whereas shallow subsiding areas can preserve richer fossil assemblages. Use environmental inference when assessing expected completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological features (denudation, faults, uplift) provide independent evidence of long time
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin's examples: great denudation of rocky piles, vertical displacements (Craven fault, Anglesea downthrow), and denudation of the Weald implying hundreds of millions of years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geomorphological and structural evidence — thickness of strata, extent of denudation, magnitude of fault displacements, and erosion rates — to infer minimum timescales available for evolutionary change; these lines of evidence support the long durations required by slow selection.
